config.title: Error Boundary

intro.title: Error Boundary
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a React component called an Error Boundary that catches JavaScript errors anywhere in its child component tree. You'll learn how to implement the componentDidCatch lifecycle method to handle errors gracefully and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the entire application. The main technologies involved are React class components and lifecycle methods. By the end, you'll understand how to create robust React applications that provide better user experiences when unexpected errors occur.
intro.usecase: Error boundaries are essential in production React applications where components can fail unpredictably. In e-commerce dashboards, they prevent a single faulty product card from crashing the entire product grid. In financial applications, they isolate errors in live data feeds while keeping the main trading interface functional. Social media platforms use them to contain failures in comment threads or media players without breaking the entire post. This pattern gives developers control over failure states while maintaining core user experience.

objectives: Implement an Error Boundary component using class syntax
Configure the Error Boundary to catch errors in its child component tree
Render fallback UI when errors are caught by the Error Boundary
Initialize state to track error status within the Error Boundary
Apply the Error Boundary to wrap components that may throw errors
Manipulate component hierarchy to isolate error-prone sections
Update existing React applications with Error Boundary protection

steps.title: Import React and Component from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and Component from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to bring in both React and Component.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing multiple items from a package
import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have access to React and the Component class for creating class components.
successCriteria: React and Component are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and Component from 'react' using the correct syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import both React and Component from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the ErrorBoundary class component
steps.instruction: Define a class component named ErrorBoundary that extends Component.
steps.hint: Use the class syntax with extends Component to create a React class component.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { Component } from 'react';

// Define the ErrorBoundary class component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A class component named ErrorBoundary is created, extending Component.
successCriteria: The ErrorBoundary class component is defined and extends Component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you define a class named ErrorBoundary that extends Component.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. Please define a class component named ErrorBoundary that extends Component.

steps.title: Initialize state with hasError property
steps.instruction: Add a constructor to your ErrorBoundary class component that initializes state with a hasError property set to false.
steps.hint: In React class components, you can initialize state in the constructor using this.state = { ... }.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component will have a constructor that sets up initial state with hasError: false.
successCriteria: ErrorBoundary has a constructor that calls super(props) and initializes this.state with hasError set to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your constructor calls super(props) and sets this.state = { hasError: false }.
steps.feedbackWrong: The constructor should initialize state with hasError set to false. Check the syntax for class component constructors.

steps.title: Implement getDerivedStateFromError lifecycle method
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary class, add the static getDerivedStateFromError method that returns { hasError: true }.
steps.hint: This static method receives the error as a parameter and should return an object to update the component's state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a static getDerivedStateFromError method that will update state when an error occurs in child components.
successCriteria: The ErrorBoundary class contains a static getDerivedStateFromError method that returns { hasError: true }.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added the static getDerivedStateFromError method that returns { hasError: true }. Remember it should be a static method inside the class.
steps.feedbackWrong: The getDerivedStateFromError method is missing or incorrect. It should be a static method that returns { hasError: true } when an error occurs.

steps.title: Implement componentDidCatch lifecycle method
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary class component, add the componentDidCatch lifecycle method that logs the error and errorInfo to the console.
steps.hint: The method should take two parameters: error and errorInfo. Use console.log to output both values.
steps.expectedOutcome: The componentDidCatch method is added to the ErrorBoundary class, logging error details to the console.
successCriteria: The componentDidCatch method is defined with parameters error and errorInfo, and logs both to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your componentDidCatch method logs both the error and errorInfo parameters to the console.
steps.feedbackWrong: The componentDidCatch method is missing or doesn't log the error information properly. Check the method signature and console.log statement.

steps.title: Add conditional rendering logic in render method
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary class, add a render method that checks if hasError is true and returns fallback UI, otherwise returns the children.
steps.hint: Use an if statement or ternary operator to conditionally render based on this.state.hasError. Return this.props.children when there's no error.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a render method that conditionally renders fallback UI when an error occurs, or renders children normally.
successCriteria: render method exists in ErrorBoundary class
returns fallback UI when hasError is true
returns this.props.children when hasError is false
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your render method checks this.state.hasError and returns appropriate content for both true and false cases.
steps.feedbackWrong: The render method is missing or doesn't properly handle the error state. Review the conditional rendering pattern.

steps.title: Create fallback UI for error state
steps.instruction: Inside the render method, return JSX that shows a user-friendly error message when hasError is true.
steps.hint: Use a conditional statement to check this.state.hasError and return appropriate JSX when it's true.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component will display a fallback UI when an error occurs in its child components.
successCriteria: The render method contains conditional logic that returns JSX with an error message when hasError is true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to check this.state.hasError and return appropriate JSX when it's true.
steps.feedbackWrong: The render method doesn't yet contain the conditional logic for displaying error messages.

steps.title: Return children when no error exists
steps.instruction: In the render method, return this.props.children when hasError is false.
steps.hint: Use a conditional statement to check this.state.hasError. If it's false, return this.props.children.
steps.expectedOutcome: The render method now returns the children when there is no error.
successCriteria: The render method conditionally returns this.props.children when hasError is false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning this.props.children when hasError is false.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the conditional logic in your render method. You need to return this.props.children when hasError is false.

steps.title: Create a BuggyComponent that throws an error
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named BuggyComponent that throws an error when rendered.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function called BuggyComponent. Inside its body, use throw new Error() with a descriptive message.
steps.expectedOutcome: A BuggyComponent function that intentionally throws an error when rendered.
successCriteria: BuggyComponent is defined as a function or arrow function and throws an error in its body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a component, but make sure it throws an error inside the function body.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating a function named BuggyComponent that throws an error when called.

steps.title: Wrap BuggyComponent with ErrorBoundary
steps.instruction: In the main App component, wrap the BuggyComponent with ErrorBoundary tags.
steps.hint: Place the BuggyComponent between opening and closing ErrorBoundary tags to make it a child of the ErrorBoundary.
steps.analogousExample:
// Wrapping a component with a wrapper
<Wrapper>
  <ChildComponent />
</Wrapper>
steps.expectedOutcome: The BuggyComponent is now wrapped by the ErrorBoundary, so any errors thrown by BuggyComponent will be caught by the boundary.
successCriteria: BuggyComponent is placed inside ErrorBoundary tags in the main App.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure BuggyComponent is directly inside the ErrorBoundary tags.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've wrapped BuggyComponent with opening and closing ErrorBoundary tags.

steps.title: Add a button to trigger the error
steps.instruction: In your BuggyComponent, add a button with an onClick handler that sets state to trigger an error when clicked.
steps.hint: You'll need to add a button element with onClick={this.triggerError} (or your handler name) inside the render method of BuggyComponent.
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Trigger Error' (or similar) appears in the BuggyComponent, and clicking it will cause the component to throw an error.
successCriteria: BuggyComponent contains a button with an onClick handler that updates state to trigger the error condition.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your button has an onClick handler that updates the state property that triggers the error in the render method.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button or its click handler is missing or incorrect. Remember to add a button element with onClick={this.triggerError} (or similar) that sets state to trigger the error.

steps.title: Add reset functionality to ErrorBoundary
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary's fallback UI, add a button with an onClick handler that calls a reset method to reset the hasError state.
steps.hint: Create a method in the ErrorBoundary class that sets hasError back to false, then add a button in the fallback UI that triggers this method.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary will have a reset method and a button in its fallback UI that allows users to reset the error state and try again.
successCriteria: ErrorBoundary has a reset method that sets hasError to false, and the fallback UI includes a button with onClick calling this method.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both the reset method and the button in the fallback UI are correctly implemented.
steps.feedbackWrong: The reset functionality is not fully implemented. Check that you've added both the reset method and the button with the onClick handler.
